<reason>B (PRO) built the more durable path. From the opening, B framed the motion as modest — it costs an afternoon and blocks only mandates no one can explain — and never let that frame be dislodged. B's decisive move was converting A's own examples into proof of feasibility: hallway questions, juniors learning by proximity, even A's late "be there so the floor is alive" were all shown to be writable, checkable mechanism-sentences, which is all the motion demands. A's strongest material was genuinely good: the density/commons argument (presence benefits flow to others, not to one's own role) and the theater-or-paralysis dilemma were the debate's best original contributions and gave A a live route. But the dilemma largely attacked a target B never defended — B had operationalized "role-specific" as "named who/whom/mechanism, checkable against observable fact, no referee needed" since B1.2, so density claims pass under B's own reading and the "paralysis" horn depends on a veto regime B explicitly disclaimed. Meanwhile B's attrition weighing (cheap information before vs. expensive, garbled information after, with the most marketable leaving first) was never effectively countered. Both sides executed format cleanly (Q1/Q2, A1/A2 labels, no fake sourcing, disciplined closings), and A's rebuttals were sharp and adaptive. B wins because its central burden survived the exchange more intact and its answers to A's best pressure fit the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 [B2.1-B2.2]: "CON hasn't defended broad assertions; it has demonstrated how easy role-specific justification is" — turning A's analyst example into the concession-hunting frame that A never escaped for the rest of the debate, reinforced in B4.5 and the closing.</best_rebuttal>
